newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: NATO urges Bosnian leaders to comply with treaty.
newsitem.headline: NATO urges Bosnian leaders to comply with treaty.

text.p: NATO ministers angrily accused Bosnian leaders on Thursday of failing to comply with the terms of the 1995 Dayton peace accord and warned that the allies' patience was wearing thin.

"We express our serious concern at the lack of determination by the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina to honour their obligations," NATO foreign ministers said in a final communique issued after meeting at a luxury resort outside Lisbon.

The North Atlantic Council, the body that sets NATO policy, reaffirmed its commitment to the Bosnian peace process and stated that the failure of the parties to fulfill all the treaty's provisions "cannot be tolerated."

NATO officials will have a chance to apply pressure directly on Friday, when the three members of Bosnia's revolving presidency -- Alija Izetbegovic, Kresimir Zubak and Momcilo Krajisnik -- meet in Sintra with a multi-national peacekeeping council.
In addition, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright will travel to Bosnia this weekend amid growing international concern that the peace treaty that ended a bitter ethnic war may be unraveling.

Under the U.S.-brokered agreement, Bosnia is supposed to be a single state comprising autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat territories. But the inter-ethnic central cabinet and presidency have failed to carry out most of the major peace provisions.
Few refugees have been able to return to their homes, and the delivery of reconstruction aid has been held up by disputes among rival ethnic leaders.
While the Sintra summit focused largely on NATO's plans to expand eastward into countries of the former Soviet bloc, ministers also resolved to take a tougher line in talks with Bosnian leaders.
"We have to put huge pressure on them," German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told reporters. "The dragging out of the peace process needs clear reaction from us."
"The immediate priority must be to persuade all three ethnic groups in Bosnia that they have got to live up to the commitments they made in Dayton," British Foreign Minister Robin Cook said.

Albright, who has called for renewed efforts to enforce the peace treaty, told fellow ministers they should condition aid on compliance with the peace accord, including requirements to hand over indicted war criminals to a special tribunal in The Hague.
The presence of a 30,000-strong NATO-led peacekeeping force is considered vital to maintaining order in Bosnia, but the troops are scheduled to be pulled out in mid-1998.
